reading_md:
## Data quality checks and safe maths

Before you report a number, check the data it comes from. Voltmarkt's raw tables carry the note "This table may hold errors", and they do: some order lines were sent twice, one store's June 2024 prices were loaded in cents, some products have a missing category_id, and some price windows overlap. A query on raw data runs without a warning and gives a confident, wrong total. A check finds the problem first and tells you how big it is.

### A check returns what it found

A data-quality query reports: a count of the bad rows, the list of keys that fail, or one row per check with a pass or fail column. It does not return a cleaned copy of the table. The question says what "wrong" means, for example "a unit price more than 10 times the product's cost is in cents".

### Duplicates

A resent order line has a new order_line_id but repeats every other column. So `COUNT(DISTINCT order_line_id)` finds nothing: each copy has an ID of its own. Group by the columns that make a record instead, and keep the groups with more than one row:

`GROUP BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_eur, promo_id, line_discount_eur HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`

GROUP BY puts two missing promo_id values in one group, so copies with no promotion are found too; a join with `=` on promo_id would miss them. Each group of n lines holds one real line and n - 1 copies. Two lines of one product in one order with different quantities are two real lines, not a copy.

### Safe ratios

A ratio needs a denominator that is not 0. `x / NULLIF(y, 0)` turns a 0 denominator into a missing value, so the ratio is missing instead of an error or Infinity. A missing ratio means "nothing to measure", which is not the same as 0: a store with no lines has no copy share, not a share of 0. Wrapping the ratio in `COALESCE(..., 0)` hides that, and an average of the ratios then comes out too low. Use 0 only when the question says so.

Keep the decimals too: divide with `/`, and multiply by `100.0` for a percentage. `//`, or two whole numbers divided on PostgreSQL, drops everything after the decimal point.

### A check report

Stack one count per check with UNION ALL, each with the same columns, then turn the counts into a result:

`CASE WHEN n_bad = 0 THEN 'pass' ELSE 'fail' END`

When a share can be missing, test `IS NULL` first: a comparison with a missing value is never true.

### Reconcile to a known total

When finance states a figure, compare yours with it: return the figure as stored, the figure after the fix, and the gap or a pass or fail. A gap of 0 after the fix tells you the fix is the whole story.
syntax_md:
```sql
WITH line_sets AS (                                   -- one row per set of matching lines
  SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS n_lines                -- metrics
  FROM order_lines                                    -- source: the raw table
  GROUP BY order_id, product_id, quantity,            -- output grain: every column
           unit_price_eur, promo_id, line_discount_eur  -- but order_line_id
)
SELECT SUM(n_lines - 1) AS n_copies,                  -- copies: each set's size minus 1
       SUM(n_lines - 1) / NULLIF(SUM(n_lines), 0) AS copy_share   -- safe ratio
FROM line_sets;
```

- Duplicates: GROUP BY the columns that make a record, HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
- Ratios: `x / NULLIF(y, 0)`; keep a missing ratio missing.
- A check report: one row per check, `CASE WHEN n_bad = 0 THEN 'pass' ELSE 'fail' END`.
dialect_note: Division by zero differs by engine: in DuckDB 1 / 0 gives Infinity (inf, checked on DuckDB 1.5.6), PostgreSQL stops with an error, and SQLite returns a missing value. x / NULLIF(y, 0) returns a missing value on all of them. Dividing two whole numbers keeps the decimals in DuckDB but drops them in PostgreSQL and SQLite, so multiply by 1.0 or use a decimal before you divide.

worked_examples.title: Resent copies for each store
worked_examples.prompt: For each store, how many order lines are resent copies? This table may hold errors: two lines are copies of one order line when every column but order_line_id matches. Return store_code and n_copies for each store with at least one copy.

clauses.text: WITH line_sets AS (SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS n_lines  -- one row per set of matching lines
clauses.why: The first step counts how many lines share one set of values.
One row per order line as stored, copies included.

clauses.text: GROUP BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_eur, promo_id, line_discount_eur)
clauses.why: Every column but order_line_id, so a copy lands in the same group as its original.
A set of n lines holds one real line, so n - 1 of them are copies.

clauses.text: FROM line_sets ls JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = ls.order_id JOIN stores s ON s.store_id = o.store_id
clauses.why: Each set belongs to one order, and each order to one store.
Only the stores with at least one copy stay.

worked_examples.title: Units per order for each store, safely
worked_examples.prompt: For each store, how many units did an order hold on average in June 2024? The average is missing for a store with no June 2024 orders. Return store_code and units_per_order.

clauses.text: WITH june_orders AS (SELECT o.store_id, o.order_id, SUM(ol.quantity) AS units  -- one row per June 2024 order
clauses.why: The first step adds up each order's units.

clauses.text: FROM orders o JOIN order_lines ol ON ol.order_id = o.order_id
clauses.why: One row per order line, each with its order.

clauses.text: WHERE o.order_ts >= TIMESTAMP '2024-06-01' AND o.order_ts < TIMESTAMP '2024-07-01'
clauses.why: June 2024, from the first day up to but not including 1 July.

clauses.text: SELECT s.store_code, SUM(j.units) / NULLIF(COUNT(j.order_id), 0) AS units_per_order
clauses.why: NULLIF turns a zero order count into a missing value, so the average is missing, not Infinity.

clauses.text: FROM stores s LEFT JOIN june_orders j ON j.store_id = s.store_id
clauses.why: The LEFT JOIN keeps a store with no June orders, which then has nothing to divide.

why_clause.clause: GROUP BY order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price_eur, promo_id, line_discount_eur)
why_clause.stem: Why does the first step group by every column except order_line_id?

options.text: A resent copy has a new order_line_id, so only the other columns show that two lines are the same order line.
order_line_id is the primary key, and GROUP BY may not use a primary key column.
Grouping by order_line_id too would merge each copy with its original and hide it.
COUNT(*) only counts the lines when every other column is in the GROUP BY.

why_clause.explanation: The copy repeats every value of the original line except its order_line_id, which is new. Grouping by the other columns puts the two in one group of 2. Adding order_line_id would split them again, one group per line, so no copy would show. GROUP BY may name any column, and COUNT(*) counts the rows of each group whatever you group by.
